title: The Aeneid — from Burning Troy to Latium
years: c. 1184-1177 BC (traditional; the fall of Troy to the founding of the Roman line)
register: national mythology — the canon is true

segments.name: The Last Night of Troy — Ilium in Flames

stops.name: Troy — the shore, and the horse brought within the walls
stops.campa: The tenth year turns and the Greeks are gone — only a monstrous horse of pine stands on the empty shore, an offering, they say, to Pallas. Laocoön the priest hurls his spear into its flank and the hollow belly groans. He cries out against the gift, but the crowd will not hear. The Trojans breach their own wall, drag the great engine up the slope with ropes and rollers, and set it, garlanded, in the heart of the citadel. Four times it halts at the threshold; four times the arms within clash — and no one listens.
stops.quote: Equo ne credite, Teucri. / Quidquid id est, timeo Danaos et dona ferentis.
suggested_refs: Laocoön and His Sons (Vatican marble, Hellenistic)
El Greco — Laocoön (1610-14)
The Trojan Horse — Pompeii fresco, House of Menander

stops.name: The altar of the household gods — the serpents from Tenedos
stops.campa: Two serpents come coiling over the calm sea from Tenedos, breasts high above the swell, blood-red crests raised. They make straight for Laocoön, seize first his two small sons, then the father who runs to help — winding twice about his waist, twice about his throat, their heads reared over him. He strains to tear the knots, his priestly fillets soaked with venom and black gore, and his cry goes up to the stars like a wounded bull's. The people read the sign backward: the horse is holy, and Laocoön died for his impiety. So the city dooms itself.
stops.quote: Ille simul manibus tendit divellere nodos / clamores simul horrendos ad sidera tollit.
suggested_refs: Laocoön Group, Vatican Museums
Aeneid Book 2 illustrations, Vergilius Vaticanus (5th c. manuscript)

stops.name: The ghost of Hector in the sleeping house
stops.campa: As the Greeks pour from the horse's belly and fire runs through Ilium, Aeneas sleeps, and Hector comes to him in dream — not the Hector who drove Greek fleets with torches, but torn and black with dust, his beard matted, thonged as he was when Achilles dragged him behind the chariot. He weeps. He tells Aeneas Troy is falling and lays upon him the sacred charge: take the Penates, the household gods, and flee to found new walls across the sea. Aeneas wakes to a city already burning.
stops.quote: Heu fuge, nate dea, teque his, ait, eripe flammis. / Hostis habet muros; ruit alto a culmine Troia.
suggested_refs: The Shade of Hector Appearing to Aeneas — Vergilius Romanus miniature
Dosso Dossi — Aeneas and the ghost of Hector

stops.name: The flight from Troy — Anchises on his shoulders, Ascanius at his hand, Creusa lost
stops.campa: Priam is dead at his own altar; Neoptolemus has slain the old king before the queen's eyes. A tongue of flame licks harmless about young Ascanius's hair — an omen — and thunder answers on the left. Aeneas lifts his crippled father Anchises onto his shoulders, sets little Iulus's hand in his own, and bids Creusa follow behind. They pass through smoke and slaughter to the gate. But Creusa is lost in the dark. He runs back through the burning streets calling her name, and only her cold shade answers, foretelling long exile, a western land, a royal bride upon the Tiber.
stops.quote: Ergo age, care pater, cervici imponere nostrae; / ipse subibo umeris nec me labor iste gravabit.
suggested_refs: Bernini — Aeneas, Anchises, and Ascanius (Galleria Borghese, 1618-19)
Federico Barocci — Aeneas' Flight from Troy (1598, Galleria Borghese)
Pompeii fresco of Aeneas carrying Anchises

stops.name: Antandros — building the fleet beneath Mount Ida
stops.campa: At the foot of Phrygian Ida, in the port of Antandros, the survivors fell timber and build a fleet, uncertain where fate is driving them. Through the first summer after the fall they lay keels and rig ships beneath the mountain that gave Troy her pine. When the first sailing weather comes and Anchises bids them trust the wind, Aeneas launches, weeping, and leaves behind the shore of his fathers, the plains where Troy once stood, an exile with his comrades, his son, and the great gods of his house.
stops.quote: Litora cum patriae lacrimans portusque relinquo / et campos ubi Troia fuit.
suggested_refs: Mount Ida (Kaz Dağı) National Park, Turkey
Antandros archaeological site, Altınoluk

segments.name: The Wandering of the Seven Years — Book Three

stops.name: Thrace — the bleeding bush of Polydorus
stops.campa: On the Thracian coast, land once friendly to Troy, Aeneas begins to trace the walls of a first city, Aeneadae. He goes to tear green boughs from a mound to dress the altars — and from the broken shoots black blood drips upon the ground. He wrenches a second, a third; the earth groans, and a voice comes up from the barrow: it is Polydorus, Priam's youngest son, sent here for safekeeping with Troy's gold and murdered by the treacherous king, his body pierced by the spears that took root and grew into this thicket. Aeneas gives him due burial and flees the accursed shore.
stops.quote: Quid miserum, Aenea, laceras? Iam parce sepulto, / parce pias scelerare manus.
suggested_refs: Ainos / Enez, Thrace (Turkey)
Vergilius Vaticanus — Aeneas and the bleeding shrub

stops.name: Delos — the oracle of Apollo and the ancient mother
stops.campa: The floating island Ortygia, which Apollo anchored, receives the Trojans; King Anius, priest and old friend of Anchises, greets them. Aeneas prays at the god's threshold, and the whole shrine trembles — the laurel, the mountain, the tripod. The voice bids them seek the ancient mother, the land from which the race of Dardanus first sprang: there their house shall lord it over all shores. Anchises, remembering wrongly, reads the oracle as Crete, where Teucer once ruled, and turns the prows south.
stops.quote: Dardanidae duri, quae vos a stirpe parentum / prima tulit tellus, eadem vos ubere laeto / accipiet reduces. Antiquam exquirite matrem.
suggested_refs: Sacred Way and Temple of Apollo, Delos (UNESCO)
Terrace of the Lions, Delos

stops.name: Crete — Pergamea, the plague, and the Penates' vision
stops.campa: On Crete, the isle of a hundred cities, Aeneas lays out walls with joy and names the town Pergamea; he urges the young to love their new hearths. But heaven turns pestilent — a wasting year rots the crops, sickens the men, kills the cattle; the fields deny the plow. In the night the Penates, the sacred images he carried from the fire, stand in the moonlight at his bed and correct the error: not Crete but Hesperia, the western land the Greeks call Italy, is the true ancient mother, the home of Dardanus and of Iasius. There lies Rome to be.
stops.quote: Est locus, Hesperiam Grai cognomine dicunt, / terra antiqua, potens armis atque ubere glaebae.
suggested_refs: Palace of Knossos, Crete
Vergilius Romanus — the Penates appearing to Aeneas

stops.name: The Strophades — the Harpies and Celaeno's prophecy
stops.campa: Storm-driven, they make the Strophades in the Ionian sea, home of the Harpies — birds with maidens' faces, filth dripping from their bellies, hands hooked, a hunger nothing sates. The Trojans slaughter cattle on the shore and set the feast; twice the foul flock swoops shrieking and fouls the tables. They fight them off with swords, but the birds cannot be wounded. From a high rock Celaeno, eldest of the Harpies, croaks a curse: they will reach Italy, but famine so bitter will hound them that they shall gnaw their very tables before they wall their city.
stops.quote: Italiam cursu petitis... / sed non ante datam cingetis moenibus urbem / quam vos dira fames... / ambesas subigat malis absumere mensas.
suggested_refs: Strofades islands, Ionian Sea (Greece)
François Perrier — Aeneas and his Companions Fighting the Harpies (Louvre)

stops.name: Actium — the games and the shield of Abas
stops.campa: Past Zacynthos, Dulichium, Ithaca — cursing the land that bred Ulysses — they gain the harbor of Actium under Apollo's cape. Here at last they rest and hold Ilian games, oiled and wrestling in the ancestral way, glad to have slipped so many Greek towns unseen. On the temple doorpost Aeneas nails a hollow shield of bronze once borne by great Abas, and cuts the line: AENEAS THESE ARMS FROM THE CONQUERING GREEKS. Then the north wind calls and they leave the leader of the Leucadians and the altars dreaded by sailors.
stops.quote: Aeneas haec de Danais victoribus arma.
suggested_refs: Actium promontory, Ambracian Gulf (Greece)
Nikopolis, founded by Augustus at Actium

stops.name: Buthrotum — Andromache, little Troy, and Helenus's prophecy
stops.campa: At Buthrotum Aeneas finds a marvel: a Troy rebuilt in miniature, a dry brook named Xanthus, a Scaean gate. Helenus, Priam's prophet-son, now reigns; Andromache, Hector's widow, pours wine at an empty tomb to her lost husband's ghost. She sees Aeneas and nearly faints, then weeps to touch a living Trojan and Ascanius, so like her own dead Astyanax. Helenus, seer of Apollo, unfolds the long road: shun the near Italian coast full of Greeks, round Sicily, seek the Sibyl at Cumae, and know the omen — a white sow with thirty white young — that marks the destined place.
stops.quote: Cum tibi sollicito secreti ad fluminis undam / litoreis ingens inventa sub ilicibus sus / triginta capitum fetus enixa iacebit... / is locus urbis erit.
stops.quote_source: Virgil, Aeneid 3.389-393 (Helenus's prophecy of the white sow)
suggested_refs: Butrint archaeological park, Albania (UNESCO)
The Lion Gate and theatre of Butrint

stops.name: Castrum Minervae — the first sight of Italy and the four white horses
stops.campa: At dawn, low on the horizon, Achates spies dim hills — Italy! The whole crew hails it, and Anchises crowns a great bowl with wine and calls on the gods of sea and storm. They put in below Minerva's temple on the height, the first Italian shore. Four snow-white horses graze the plain, and Anchises reads the omen twofold: horses mean war, yet horses broken to the car and yoke mean peace at the last. They pray, veil their heads in Trojan fashion, and — as Helenus warned — quit at once this coast that faces Greece, naming the harbor Portus Veneris.
stops.quote: Italiam primus conclamat Achates, / Italiam laeto socii clamore salutant.
suggested_refs: Castro (Apulia), ancient Castrum Minervae, Salento
The 'Aeneas of Castro' marble head, found in the temple of Athena (2015)

segments.name: The Straits and the Cyclops' Shore

stops.name: Tarentum and the Lacinian headland — skirting the gulf
stops.campa: Rounding the great gulf, they pass the bay where Herculean Tarentum lies, the temple of Lacinian Juno rising on its cape, the towers of Caulon and shipwreck-dreaded Scylaceum. Far off, sea-wet, Mount Etna comes into view. They hear the deep boom of surf on rocks and the sea beaten to spray — Anchises knows it: Charybdis. Man the oars! They swing left and away, keeping to the open water, coasting the toe of Italy before the terror of the straits.
stops.quote: Praeterea, si qua est Heleno prudentia vati... / hoc unum... praedicam.
stops.quote_source: Virgil, Aeneid 3.433-436 (Helenus, on avoiding Scylla and Charybdis)
suggested_refs: Capo Colonna, Temple of Hera Lacinia, Crotone (Calabria)
The single surviving column of the Lacinian temple

stops.name: The shore beneath Aetna — the Cyclops and Achaemenides
stops.campa: They land at nightfall beneath Aetna, which thunders and hurls balls of flame and glowing rock to the stars while the mountain groans. At dawn a wretch stumbles from the woods, ragged, starved, hands stretched out — Achaemenides, a Greek left behind by Ulysses in the Cyclops' cave. He tells of Polyphemus crunching his comrades' bones and begs to be taken, even to death, so long as it is by human hands. Then the blind giant himself comes down to the sea, a lopped pine for a staff, washing his gouged socket. The Trojans cut cable and row for their lives.
stops.quote: Monstrum horrendum, informe, ingens, cui lumen ademptum.
suggested_refs: Mount Etna, Sicily (UNESCO)
The Faraglioni / Cyclopean Isles off Aci Trezza
Guido Reni — Polyphemus

stops.name: Drepanum — the death of Anchises
stops.campa: Skirting Sicily past Pantagias, Megara's bay, Camarina, Gela, Acragas the horse-breeder, palmy Selinus, and the shallows of Lilybaeum, they reach at last the joyless harbor of Drepanum. Here, worn by so much sea, Anchises — father, comfort, the pilot of all his cares — lays down his life. No seer had warned of this grief, not dread Celaeno, not Helenus. It is the last sorrow, the end of the long road's first half. From here a storm will drive them to Africa. So Aeneas himself ends the telling of his wanderings, and falls silent.
stops.quote: Hic pelagi tot tempestatibus actus / heu, genitorem, omnis curae casusque levamen, / amitto Anchisen.
suggested_refs: Trapani (ancient Drepanum), Sicily
Mount Eryx and the temple of Venus Erycina above the harbor

segments.name: Carthage and Dido — the Tragic Queen

stops.name: The storm off the Libyan coast — Juno's wrath, Neptune's rebuke
stops.campa: Barely out of Sicily's sight, the fleet is caught. Juno, who hates the Trojan race and dreads the Rome that will one day cast down her Carthage, buys the wind-king Aeolus and looses the storms. Black night falls on the sea; three ships are hurled on hidden rocks, three on the shoals; Aeneas groans and wishes he had died at Troy. Then Neptune lifts his calm head above the waves, scolds the runaway winds, and stills the water — as a grave man quiets a rioting crowd by the weight of his presence. Seven battered ships limp toward Libya.
stops.quote: Quos ego—! Sed motos praestat componere fluctus.
stops.quote_source: Virgil, Aeneid 1.135 (Neptune to the winds — the famous unfinished threat, 'Whom I—!')
suggested_refs: Vergilius Vaticanus — the Storm and Neptune calming the sea
Rubens — The Landing of Aeneas

stops.name: The Libyan shore — Venus, the huntress, and the mist
stops.campa: In a deep cove screened by woods the survivors land; Aeneas climbs a crag, sees no ships but shoots seven great stags for the seven crews, and heartens his men — endure, keep for better days, perhaps one day it will be a joy to remember even this. His mother Venus meets him in the forest disguised as a Tyrian huntress, tells him of Dido, the widowed queen who fled her brother Pygmalion's knife and Tyre to build a new city here. Then she wraps him and Achates in a cloud so that none may stop or question them, and sends them up to the rising walls.
stops.quote: Forsan et haec olim meminisse iuvabit.
suggested_refs: Aeneas and Venus — Pietro da Cortona
Ancient shore of the Gulf of Tunis

stops.name: Carthage rising — the murals of Troy on Juno's temple
stops.campa: Where lately were huts stands a city climbing the Byrsa: Tyrians lay walls, roll up citadel-stones, dig harbors, set out laws — busy as bees in early summer. In the grove of Juno's new temple Aeneas stops astonished: the whole Trojan war is painted here — Priam, the sons of Atreus, Achilles, Hector dragged, Troilus falling from his car. The world's tears are in these images; mortal things touch the heart. He weeps to see his own griefs made famous, and takes courage: even here, at the world's edge, Troy is known and pitied.
stops.quote: Sunt hic etiam sua praemia laudi; / sunt lacrimae rerum et mentem mortalia tangunt.
suggested_refs: Byrsa Hill, Carthage (Tunisia)
The Low Ham Roman mosaic (Dido and Aeneas cycle), Somerset

stops.name: Dido's hall — the banquet and Cupid in Ascanius's shape
stops.campa: Dido, beautiful and generous, welcomes the storm-lost Trojans and Aeneas steps from the cloud like a god. At the feast Venus sends Cupid disguised as Ascanius to sit in the queen's lap; while she fondles the boy she does not know she is drinking in ruinous love, forgetting her vow to her dead husband Sychaeus. She asks Aeneas to tell the whole tale from the beginning — the fall of Troy, the seven years' wandering — and hangs upon his every word deep into the night, doomed, the fire already lit in her marrow.
stops.quote: Infandum, regina, iubes renovare dolorem.
stops.quote_source: Virgil, Aeneid 2.3 (Aeneas begins his tale to Dido)
suggested_refs: Guérin — Aeneas Telling Dido the Misfortunes of Troy (Louvre)
Dido and Aeneas — Rutilio Manetti

stops.name: The cave — the hunt, the storm, and the fatal union
stops.campa: Juno and Venus, each for her own ends, contrive it. On a royal hunt a black storm bursts; hail sweeps the ridges; the company scatters. Dido and the Trojan leader take shelter in the same cave. Lightning is their wedding-torch, the mountain nymphs cry out on the heights; earth and sky give the sign. This day is the first cause of death and of all her sorrows — for Dido no longer hides her love or calls it sin, but names it marriage. Rumor, swift and monstrous, runs through the Libyan towns: the queen and the wanderer pass the winter in soft forgetting, careless of their kingdoms.
stops.quote: Coniugium vocat, hoc praetexit nomine culpam.
stops.quote_source: Virgil, Aeneid 4.172 (of Dido after the cave)
suggested_refs: Dido and Aeneas Sheltering from the Storm — Rutilio Manetti / Nathaniel Dance-Holland
Purcell's opera Dido and Aeneas (1689)

stops.name: Mercury's command — the abandonment
stops.campa: Jupiter, angered, sends Mercury sliding down the winds to find Aeneas laying courses of stone for Carthage in a Tyrian cloak Dido gave him — building another's city, forgetting his own. The god's rebuke is stinging: what of Italy, of Ascanius's inheritance, of the Roman realm owed to fate? Aeneas is struck dumb, his hair on end. Duty conquers love. He orders the fleet made ready in secret. Dido learns — Rumor tells her — and confronts him, pleading, raging, calling him faithless. He answers that he sails not of his own will: Italy is his country now, not by choice but by the gods' command.
stops.quote: Italiam non sponte sequor.
suggested_refs: Tiepolo — Mercury Appearing to Aeneas
Dido and Aeneas — Guérin (1815, Louvre)

stops.name: The pyre — Dido's curse and the seed of Hannibal
stops.campa: At first light Dido sees the harbor empty, the sails gone. She has raised a great pyre, pretending a rite to unbind her love. From its top, holding the Trojan sword he left, she curses him: let a nameless avenger rise from her bones to hound the Dardan settlers with fire and iron — shore against shore, arms against arms, they and their children's children! Then she falls on the blade. The city wails as if all Carthage were burning. Far out at sea Aeneas looks back and sees the walls aglow with her fire. The curse is loosed; it has a name to come — Hannibal.
stops.quote: Exoriare aliquis nostris ex ossibus ultor / qui face Dardanios ferroque sequare colonos.
suggested_refs: The Death of Dido — Guercino (1631, Galleria Spada)
Sir Joshua Reynolds — The Death of Dido (1781)
Berlioz, Les Troyens — Dido's death scene

stops.name: Return to Drepanum — the games at Anchises's tomb
stops.campa: Storm turns the fleet back to friendly Sicily, to Acestes the Trojan-born king and the tomb of Anchises, a year dead. Aeneas keeps the anniversary with sacrifice — a great serpent glides from the shrine, tastes the offerings, and departs unharmed, a good omen of his father's spirit. Then he proclaims games: a ship-race won by steady Cloanthus, a footrace, the brutal boxing where old Entellus fells the boastful Dares, an archery match where Acestes's arrow catches fire in mid-air and streaks like a comet — a wonder none can read, but a sign of great things.
stops.quote: Incaluit vino, tum pectore fervidus alto / ... magnanimum Aenean.
suggested_refs: Segesta, temple and theatre (near ancient Egesta/Acesta)
Vergilius Romanus — the funeral games, Book 5

stops.name: The burning of the ships — Acesta founded, the weary left behind
stops.campa: Juno sends Iris among the tired Trojan women, sick of the endless sea; maddened, they fling fire into the hulls. Four ships burn before Jupiter answers Aeneas's prayer with sudden rain and quenches them. Shaken, Aeneas takes old Nautes's counsel: leave here the aged, the women weary of glory, all who have no heart for greatness. He founds a city, Acesta, marks out its walls and a forum, and dedicates a grove to Venus of Eryx. Lightened, the chosen sail on. In the night Anchises's shade bids him seek the Sibyl and descend to Elysium to learn his people's fate.
stops.quote: Nate, mihi vita quondam, dum vita manebat, / care magis... duc me ad tua limina.
stops.quote_source: Virgil, Aeneid 5 (Anchises's shade to Aeneas), paraphrased from 5.724ff
suggested_refs: Mount Eryx (Erice) and the sanctuary of Venus Erycina
Palinurus asleep at the helm — Book 5 close

stops.name: Cape Palinurus — the helmsman lost to the sea
stops.campa: The crossing to Italy costs one life for many. The god Sleep, in a comrade's shape, comes to Palinurus at the steering-oar and urges him to rest; the honest pilot refuses to trust the treacherous calm, but the god shakes a bough dripping Lethe over him and pitches him overboard with the tiller and part of the stern. He falls calling on his friends, and the ship sails on rudderless under Neptune's promise — one head given for the safe passage of the rest. Aeneas, waking, takes the helm himself, grieving, and names the headland for his lost steersman: Palinurus.
stops.quote: O nimium caelo et pelago confise sereno, / nudus in ignota, Palinure, iacebis harena.
suggested_refs: Capo Palinuro, Cilento coast (Campania)
Cilento and Vallo di Diano National Park (UNESCO)

segments.name: Cumae, the Sibyl, and the Descent to the Dead

stops.name: Cumae — the temple doors of Daedalus and the Sibyl's frenzy
stops.campa: They make landfall at Cumae, the Euboean shore. On the temple doors Daedalus wrought the tale of the Cretan labyrinth in gold. Aeneas seeks the vast cave of the Sibyl, with its hundred mouths. The god Apollo comes upon her; her face changes, her breast heaves, she grows taller and her voice is not mortal as the god forces her to speak. She foretells wars in Latium, a Tiber foaming with blood, a new Achilles, a foreign bride again the cause of war — yet bids him yield not but press the harder against his fate. First, though, he must go down among the dead.
stops.quote: Tu ne cede malis, sed contra audentior ito.
suggested_refs: The Cave of the Sibyl, Cuma (Campi Flegrei)
Michelangelo — Cumaean Sibyl, Sistine Chapel

stops.name: Lake Avernus — the golden bough and the gate of hell
stops.campa: To descend and return, the Sibyl says, one must first pluck the golden bough sacred to Juno of the underworld, hidden in a dark tree — it comes willingly to the fated hand, or not at all. Venus's twin doves lead Aeneas to it above the reeking chasm of Avernus, where no bird can fly and live. He breaks the gleaming branch. Beside the black lake he buries the trumpeter Misenus, slain for challenging the gods, raises his tomb on the cape that keeps his name, and stands ready at the cavern-mouth through which the way runs down to the dead.
stops.quote: Facilis descensus Averno; / ... sed revocare gradum superasque evadere ad auras, / hoc opus, hic labor est.
suggested_refs: Lake Avernus, Campi Flegrei
Turner — The Golden Bough (1834, Tate)
J.G. Frazer's The Golden Bough (title from this scene)

stops.name: The banks of Acheron — Charon and the golden bough
stops.campa: Down through the throat of the earth they go, past Grief, Cares, Diseases, pale Death, and the monstrous shapes at the gate — Centaurs, Gorgons, the Hydra. At the muddy Acheron, filthy Charon the ferryman drives off the crowd of the unburied, who stretch their hands to the far bank and must wander a hundred years. There Aeneas sees his lost helmsman Palinurus among them. The grim boatman would bar a living man, but the Sibyl lifts the golden bough from her robe; his anger melts, he draws in the boat, and the leaky hull groans under a living weight as it ferries hero and priestess across.
stops.quote: Portitor has horrendus aquas et flumina servat / terribili squalore Charon.
suggested_refs: Charon's boat — Etruscan and Roman funerary art
Patinir — Crossing the River Styx

stops.name: The Fields of Mourning — Dido's silent shade
stops.campa: In the Fields of Mourning, where those whom cruel love wasted keep to their myrtle groves, Aeneas comes upon Dido, her wound still fresh. He weeps and speaks tenderly: he did not know his going would cost her so dear; he left against his will, by the gods' command. She will not look at him; she keeps her eyes on the ground, no more moved than flint or marble, then turns away into the shadowy wood to Sychaeus her first husband, who answers her love. Aeneas, shaken and pitying, follows her a long way with his eyes and weeps for her hard fate.
stops.quote: Illa solo fixos oculos aversa tenebat / nec magis incepto vultum sermone movetur / quam si dura silex aut stet Marpesia cautes.
suggested_refs: Andrea Sacchi / Wenceslaus Hollar — Aeneas and Dido in the underworld
The Fields of Mourning, Lugentes Campi

stops.name: Elysium — Anchises and the pageant of unborn Roman souls
stops.campa: In Elysium, under its own sun and stars, among the blessed, Aeneas finds Anchises reviewing the souls of his descendants who wait by the river Lethe to be born. Three times Aeneas tries to embrace him; three times the shade slips through his hands like wind, like a dream. Then Anchises unrolls the future: he shows the line of souls that will be Rome — Silvius, Romulus, the Caesars, Augustus who will bring back a golden age, and there, the young Marcellus, marked for early death, walking in shadow. He names Rome's very art: to rule the nations, spare the conquered, and beat down the proud.
stops.quote: Tu regere imperio populos, Romane, memento / (hae tibi erunt artes), pacique imponere morem, / parcere subiectis et debellare superbos.
suggested_refs: Ingres — Virgil Reading the Aeneid (Tu Marcellus eris)
The Pageant of Heroes, Aeneid Book 6
The Ara Pacis Augustae, Rome

segments.name: Latium — the Promised Land and the War for Lavinia

stops.name: Caieta — the nurse buried on the shore
stops.campa: Sailing north from Cumae along the coast, past the isle of Circe where men once became beasts and the enchantress's song rises through the pines, Aeneas's old nurse Caieta dies. He buries her on the headland and gives it her name forever — a small human grief threaded through the great design. Neptune grants a fair wind; they pass the Circean shore by night, Venus lighting the way, and by morning the wind falls and the oars take the calm as the long-sought river comes at last into view.
stops.quote: Tu quoque litoribus nostris, Aeneia nutrix, / aeternam moriens famam, Caieta, dedisti.
suggested_refs: Gaeta (ancient Caieta), Lazio
Monte Circeo, the promontory of Circe

stops.name: The mouth of the Tiber — the promised land at last
stops.campa: At the mouth of the Tiber, amid a great wood where the river breaks yellow with sand into the sea, the Trojans put in. Weary, they lay their meal on wheaten cakes for tables and heap the crusts with wild fruit — and eat the bread beneath. Ascanius laughs: we are eating our tables! And Aeneas knows the omen fulfilled, the Harpy's curse turned to blessing: this is the place, the end of wandering, the fated home. He crowns his brow with leaves and prays to the genius of the land, to the nymphs, to the still-unknown river, and to Mother Earth. The seven years are over.
stops.quote: Heus, etiam mensas consumimus, inquit Iulus. / ... Salve fatis mihi debita tellus.
suggested_refs: Ostia and the Tiber mouth (Fiumicino/Ostia Antica), Lazio
The white sow with thirty piglets — the founding omen

stops.name: Laurentum — King Latinus, Lavinia, and the flame in her hair
stops.campa: In the city of Laurentum, old King Latinus rules the Latins in peace. His only daughter Lavinia is sought by many, above all by Turnus the Rutulian, favored by the queen Amata. But omens forbid: bees swarm on the sacred laurel, foretelling strangers who will rule; and as Lavinia stands by her father at the altar, her hair and crown catch fire — harmless flame running over her — a sign of glory for herself and war for her people. An oracle warns Latinus to wed his daughter to no Latin but to a coming foreigner. Aeneas's envoys arrive; Latinus knows the fated son-in-law has come.
stops.quote: Externi venient generi, qui sanguine nostrum / nomen in astra ferant.
stops.quote_source: Virgil, Aeneid 7.98-99 (the oracle of Faunus to Latinus)
suggested_refs: Lavinium / Pratica di Mare, sanctuary of the Thirteen Altars
The Heroon of Aeneas at Lavinium

stops.name: Pallanteum — the future site of Rome, and the shield of Aeneas
stops.campa: War kindles: Juno looses the Fury Allecto, Amata rages, Turnus arms the Latin peoples. The river-god Tiber bids Aeneas seek allies upstream, where he finds the white sow with her thirty young — the destined sign. He comes to Pallanteum, the little Arcadian town of old King Evander on the very hills where Rome will stand. Evander walks him over the future Forum and Capitol, then cattle-pasture and thicket. Venus brings arms forged by Vulcan, and on the shield are wrought all the deeds to come — down to Augustus at Actium and the triumph in Rome. Aeneas shoulders, unknowing, the whole fame and fate of his descendants.
stops.quote: Attollens umero famamque et fata nepotum.
suggested_refs: The Palatine Hill and the site of the Roman Forum

stops.name: The Latin field — the fall of Turnus and the founding of the line
stops.campa: The war rages: Nisus and Euryalus die in the night raid; young Pallas, Evander's son, falls to Turnus, who strips his sword-belt; Camilla the warrior-maid is slain. At the last the two champions meet in single combat before both armies. Aeneas wounds Turnus and stands over him with sword raised as the Rutulian pleads for his life. Aeneas wavers — until he sees on Turnus's shoulder the belt of murdered Pallas. Blazing with grief and fury, he drives the blade home: this stroke is for Pallas. Turnus's life flees groaning to the shades. So ends the poem, and so begins Rome.
stops.quote: Ast illi solvuntur frigore membra / vitaque cum gemitu fugit indignata sub umbras.
